docs.title: Adaptive Competitive Programming Pattern Retention System
docs.text:
CP Recall is a full-stack web application paired with a Tampermonkey browser extension that helps competitive programmers build long-term retention of DSA algorithmic patterns, not just individual problem solutions.

The system integrates directly into LeetCode. When a problem is solved, the extension records the solving session, sends the accepted code to an AI model for complexity analysis, computes a multi-component mastery score, and schedules a future review using a simplified FSRS-inspired scheduler — critically, the review surfaces a different, unsolved problem from the same algorithmic pattern family, testing genuine conceptual transfer rather than memorisation.

docs.title: The Core Insight
docs.text:
Most competitive programming platforms track how many problems a user has solved. CP Recall tracks how well the user has retained the pattern behind each problem.

A user who solved a Sliding Window problem three weeks ago and cannot recognise a new Sliding Window problem has not retained the concept. CP Recall detects and corrects this.

docs.title: How the System Works
docs.text:
1. Extension detects when a problem is accepted on LeetCode
  2. LLM analyses the accepted code for time and space complexity using Gemini 2.0 Flash
  3. Mastery is computed from 5 dimensions: solution efficiency, time complexity, submission count, time taken, and hints used
  4. FSRS schedules the next review interval based on the mastery score
  5. Dashboard surfaces a different, unsolved problem from the same weak pattern when the review interval matures
  6. Marking a recall as done extends the FSRS interval; failing resets it

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: CP Recall uses Google Gemini 2.0 Flash to analyse the user's accepted LeetCode solution immediately after submission. This analysis drives the Solution Efficiency and Time Complexity components of the mastery score and provides rich pedagogical feedback on the Problem Details page.

docs.title: When Analysis Runs
docs.text: The Tampermonkey extension calls POST /api/analyze with the accepted code immediately after the submission is accepted — before the full ingestion POST. The analysis result is embedded in the ingestion payload as analysisResult.

docs.title: Input to Gemini
docs.text: Field Source code Full accepted source code from LeetCode GraphQL (sent by extension) problemTitle LeetCode problem title (sent by extension) difficulty "Easy", "Medium", or "Hard" (sent by extension) language Programming language, e.g. python3, cpp (sent by extension) patterns Loaded from the Problem record in the database ([] if not yet in DB) problemDescription Lazy-loaded by analyzeController.js from LeetCode questionContent GraphQL (4s timeout) and cached on Problem.description if the problem already exists in the DB with an empty description; HTML-stripped and truncated to 3000 chars ("" if the problem is not yet in the DB)

docs.title: Output from Gemini
docs.text:
{
  "actualTimeComplexity":    "O(N)",
  "actualSpaceComplexity":   "O(1)",
  "optimalTimeComplexity":   "O(N)",
  "optimalSpaceComplexity":  "O(1)",
  "explanation":             "Linear scan with constant extra space.",
  "richAnalysis": {
    "problemUnderstanding":     "...",
    "yourApproach":             "...",
    "correctness":              "...",
    "optimalApproach":          "...",
    "comparison":               "...",
    "efficiencyAssessment":     "...",
    "improvementSuggestions":   "..."
  }
}

docs.title: Rich Analysis Fields
docs.text: Field Description problemUnderstanding What the problem requires and its key constraints yourApproach Algorithm the user used: data structures, loops, recursion correctness Logical correctness and potential edge-case issues optimalApproach Best-known solution technique for this problem type comparison Direct comparison of user's vs optimal approach efficiencyAssessment Whether the user's approach is feasible under given constraints improvementSuggestions 1–2 concrete, actionable improvements

docs.title: Complexity Validation & Fallback Impact
docs.text:
After parsing Gemini's JSON response, codeAnalysis.js validates that all four complexity fields (actualTimeComplexity, actualSpaceComplexity, optimalTimeComplexity, optimalSpaceComplexity) are present. If any field is missing or falsy, it falls back to "O(N)" to prevent null propagation.

Impact on Mastery Scoring: Because scoring.js compares complexity strings by exact equality (actualTimeComplexity === optimalTimeComplexity), an "O(N)" fallback can affect both the Solution Efficiency (25%) and Time Complexity (25%) mastery components — either penalizing a non-O(N) solution (e.g., O(1) or O(log N)) if optimalTimeComplexity fell back to "O(N)", or artificially matching if both fell back to "O(N)". If the entire JSON parse fails, the analysis endpoint throws an error.

docs.title: Model Selection Rationale
docs.text: gemini-2.0-flash was chosen for: - Latency: fast enough to call synchronously before the ingestion POST - Structured output: reliable JSON formatting for complexity analysis tasks - Cost: efficient token usage for code analysis at this scale

docs.title: Where Results Are Displayed
docs.text: The richAnalysis object is stored in AcceptedSolution.analysisResult and displayed on the Problem Details page under the AI Code Analysis panel. The complexity fields drive the Solution Efficiency and Time Complexity mastery component scores.

docs.title: Authentication Mechanism
docs.text: CP Recall uses JWT (JSON Web Token) based stateless authentication.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
1. User submits name, email, and password via POST /api/auth/register
  2. The User model's pre-save hook hashes the password with bcrypt (10 salt rounds)
  3. A JWT is generated and returned; the user is immediately logged in

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
1. User submits email and password via POST /api/auth/login
  2. The backend fetches the user record (with passwordHash explicitly selected, since select: false excludes it by default)
  3. bcrypt.compare() validates the password
  4. A JWT signed with JWT_SECRET (7-day expiry) is returned

docs.title: Session Management
docs.text:
The JWT is stored and used across two contexts: - Dashboard (Web App): Set in an HTTP-only cookie by the server (which restricts JavaScript from reading the cookie directly via document.cookie) and also stored in localStorage as cprecall_token for Authorization: Bearer requests and extension-key copying. AuthContext hydrates from localStorage on mount and verifies against GET /api/auth/me (clearing stale state on 401 without logging out on transient errors).

Security note: While the HTTP-only cookie prevents direct script access to the cookie itself, it does not provide complete XSS protection—particularly because the dashboard JWT is also stored in localStorage, which is readable by any JavaScript executing on the same origin. - Tampermonkey Extension (code/extension/cp-recal.user.js): Has no independent login flow. After logging into the dashboard, the user clicks the Extension Key button in TopHeader.jsx to copy their JWT, pastes it into the extension widget's Extension Key input on LeetCode, and clicks Save. The script persists it in Tampermonkey storage (GM_setValue("cprecall_sync_token", val)) and sends it via Authorization: Bearer <token> using GM_xmlhttpRequest (bypassing leetcode.com CSP and cookie restrictions).

docs.title: requireAuth Middleware
docs.text:
// 1. Check HTTP-only cookie first
let token = req.cookies?.token;

// 2. Fall back to Authorization: Bearer (for extension on leetcode.com)
if (!token && req.headers.authorization?.startsWith('Bearer ')) {
  token = req.headers.authorization.split(' ')[1];
}

// 3. Verify and attach user to request
const decoded = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET);
req.user = { userId: decoded.userId };

docs.title: CORS Policy
docs.text:
In code/server/src/app.js, the server explicitly allows origins: - process.env.CLIENT_URL (defaults to http://localhost:5173) - https://cprecall.vercel.app (legacy/alternative origin) - https://leetcode.com and https://www.leetcode.com (Tampermonkey extension)

Requests with no Origin header (e.g. GM_xmlhttpRequest, server-to-server, curl) are also permitted. All other browser origins are rejected with a CORS error.

docs.title: Route Protection
docs.text:
• Public routes: /api/auth/register, /api/auth/login, /api/auth/logout, /api/ingestion/health, GET /api/health
  • All other routes: protected by requireAuth

docs.title: Data Isolation
docs.text: Every user-scoped database query in the service layer filters by userId extracted from the verified JWT (req.user.userId). In addition, ProblemMastery, FSRSState, and AcceptedSolution enforce {userId, problemId} unique compound indexes, and PatternMastery enforces a {userId, pattern} unique compound index, while event collections (SolvingSession, Submission, ReviewHistory) index userId for scoped queries.

docs.title: Stack
docs.text: Node.js (ESM modules), Express.js 4.x, running on port 5000 by default.

docs.title: Middleware Chain
docs.text:
Every request passes through: 1. cors() — allows CLIENT_URL (default http://localhost:5173), https://cprecall.vercel.app (legacy/alternative origin), https://leetcode.com, and https://www.leetcode.com 2. express.json() — parses JSON body 3. cookieParser() — parses HTTP-only cookies

Protected routes additionally pass through requireAuth, which validates the JWT from either req.cookies.token or Authorization: Bearer <token> header.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Centralised error middleware handles: - 409 Conflict: DynamoDB ConditionalCheckFailedException, Mongoose code: 11000 - 400 Bad Request: Mongoose ValidationError - 401 Unauthorized: JWT TokenExpiredError or invalid token - 5xx: generic Internal Server Error

Unmatched routes return 404 Route not found.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
CP Recall uses a database abstraction layer controlled by the DB_BACKEND environment variable:

Value Backend mongodb (default) Mongoose ORM against MongoDB Atlas dynamodb Custom repository layer against AWS DynamoDB DUAL_WRITE=true Writes go to both; reads come from primary

This design enabled iterative migration from MongoDB (rapid prototyping) to DynamoDB (scalable, serverless production) without changing the service layer logic.

The backend defines 9 Mongoose models (User, Problem, ProblemMastery, PatternMastery, FSRSState, SolvingSession, Submission, AcceptedSolution, ReviewHistory) and 10 DynamoDB repositories: 9 repositories mapping 1-to-1 to those models (userRepo, problemRepo, problemMasteryRepo, patternMasteryRepo, fsrsStateRepo, solvingSessionRepo, submissionRepo, acceptedSolutionRepo, reviewHistoryRepo), plus progressResetRepo.js, which manages DynamoDB-specific atomic progress-reset locks and execution state rather than a standalone Mongoose model.

docs.title: User
docs.text:
Field Type Notes name String max 50 chars email String unique, lowercase, validated passwordHash String bcrypt; select: false — never returned in queries

Indexes: email (unique)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Global, shared catalog of LeetCode problems. Populated on first solve by any user.

Field Type Notes leetcodeId Number unique — LeetCode's numeric problem ID title String e.g. "Two Sum" titleSlug String unique, lowercase — used to build LeetCode URLs difficulty Enum "Easy", "Medium", "Hard" patterns [String] DSA pattern tags assigned by the extension description String Problem statement HTML (default ""; not sent by the extension or ingestion pipeline — lazy-loaded from LeetCode questionContent GraphQL by POST /api/analyze if the problem already exists in the DB without a description)

Indexes: leetcodeId (unique), titleSlug (unique), difficulty, patterns

docs.title: ProblemMastery
docs.text:
Per-user mastery record for a solved problem. One record per (user, problem).

Field Type Notes userId ObjectId scoped to user problemId ObjectId — solvingSessionId ObjectId — acceptedSubmissionId ObjectId — totalSubmissions Number total attempts including failures totalTimeSeconds Number session duration in seconds hintsUsedCount Number — solvedAt Date timestamp of accepted submission components Object 5 scores: solutionEfficiency, timeComplexity, submissionsUntilSuccess, timeTaken, hintsUsed (each 0–100) mastery Number weighted final score 0–100

Indexes: {userId, problemId} (unique), {userId, mastery: -1}, {userId}

docs.title: PatternMastery
docs.text:
Per-user mastery aggregated at the pattern level. Recomputed after every new solve.

Field Type Notes userId ObjectId — pattern String DSA pattern name totalProblemsAttempted Number — totalProblemsSolved Number — mastery Number weighted average of ProblemMastery records for this pattern components Object average of 5 component scores across solved problems in this pattern

Indexes: {userId, pattern} (unique), {userId, mastery: -1}, {userId}

docs.title: FSRSState
docs.text:
Tracks the spaced-repetition schedule for each solved problem (the trigger, Problem A).

Field Type Notes userId ObjectId — problemId ObjectId trigger problem rating Enum [1,2,3,4] derived from mastery score nextReviewDate Date when to next surface a recall intervalDays Number current interval easeFactor Number default 2.5, min 1.3 reviewHistory [{reviewedAt, rating, intervalBefore}] audit trail

Indexes: {userId, problemId} (unique), {userId, nextReviewDate}, {userId}

docs.title: SolvingSession
docs.text:
Field Type Notes userId ObjectId — problemId ObjectId — startTime Date when user opened the problem endTime Date when submission was accepted totalTimeSeconds Number computed: endTime − startTime

Indexes: {userId, problemId, startTime: -1}, {userId}, {problemId} (non-unique; multiple sessions allowed per user/problem)

docs.title: Submission
docs.text:
One record per individual submission attempt within a session.

Field Type Notes userId, problemId, sessionId ObjectId — submissionId String LeetCode's submission ID status String "Accepted", "Wrong Answer", "Time Limit Exceeded", etc. runtime, memory String LeetCode's reported values language String e.g. "Python3", "C++" timestamp Date —

Indexes: {userId, problemId}, {sessionId}, {userId} (non-unique; multiple attempts per session/problem)

docs.title: AcceptedSolution
docs.text:
Stores the final accepted code and AI analysis. One record per (user, problem). Upserted on re-solve — later solves overwrite earlier ones.

Field Type Notes userId, problemId, submissionId ObjectId — code String full accepted source code language, runtime, memory String — analysisResult Object full Gemini response (complexities + richAnalysis) solvedAt Date —

Indexes: {userId, problemId} (unique), {userId}

docs.title: ReviewHistory
docs.text:
Audit trail of mastery changes.

Field Type Notes userId, problemId ObjectId — reviewedAt Date — previousMastery Number mastery before this solve newMastery Number mastery after this solve fsrsRating Number — status String "completed"

Indexes: {userId, reviewedAt: -1}, {userId, problemId}, {userId} (non-unique; audit log of review events)

docs.title: Entity Relationships
docs.text:
User ──┬── ProblemMastery ──── Problem
       ├── FSRSState ──────────┘
       ├── SolvingSession ─────┘
       ├── Submission ─────────┘
       ├── AcceptedSolution ───┘
       ├── ReviewHistory ──────┘
       └── PatternMastery (user-pattern aggregate computed from ProblemMastery + Problem.patterns)

User-scoped collections enforce per-user isolation by scoping queries to userId from the JWT. Specifically, ProblemMastery, FSRSState, and AcceptedSolution carry unique compound indexes on {userId, problemId}, and PatternMastery carries a unique compound index on {userId, pattern}; event/history collections (SolvingSession, Submission, ReviewHistory) use non-unique indexes so multiple attempts and review records can be stored per user and problem.

docs.title: Application Deployment (AWS EC2)
docs.text:
The live CP Recall application (both the React frontend and Express.js backend API) is deployed on AWS EC2 at:

http://cprecall.duckdns.org

  • AWS Region: Unspecified (not verified from deployment infrastructure; .env.example contains ap-southeast-2 only as an example placeholder).
  • Transport Protocol: The confirmed URL uses plain HTTP (http://cprecall.duckdns.org), not HTTPS; traffic to this endpoint is not TLS-encrypted in transit.
  • Frontend build command: npm run build (Vite production build, output to dist/).
  • Backend start command: node src/server.js. The server binds to the port immediately at startup and initialises the database connection in the background.

Note on earlier/alternative deployment references in the codebase: Comments in code/extension/cp-recal.user.js, code/server/src/app.js CORS, and the 502/504 retry handler in code/client/src/services/api.js reference earlier Vercel (cprecall.vercel.app) and Render (cprecall-api.onrender.com) targets. The confirmed live deployment URL is http://cprecall.duckdns.org on AWS EC2.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Environment Backend Development MongoDB Atlas (via MONGODB_URI) or DynamoDB Local Production AWS DynamoDB (via DB_BACKEND=dynamodb + AWS_* credentials; region unspecified)

The DynamoDB problem catalog (problemRepo.initCatalog()) is loaded into server memory at startup, eliminating repeated remote reads for high-frequency pattern-matching queries in selectRecallTargets.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: All sensitive configuration is managed through environment variables and must never be committed to the repository. See Setup for the full list. The .env.example file in code/server/ documents all required variables with placeholder values.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The CP Recall browser extension is a Tampermonkey userscript (v3.1.0) located in this repository at code/extension/cp-recal.user.js. It runs on https://leetcode.com/problems/* and https://www.leetcode.com/problems/* and serves as the system's primary data collection interface.

By default, the script targets the AWS-deployed backend and frontend at http://cprecall.duckdns.org (BACKEND_URL and FRONTEND_URL).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Install the Tampermonkey extension in a Chromium-based browser or Firefox.
  2. Open the Tampermonkey dashboard and create a new userscript.
  3. Copy the contents of code/extension/cp-recal.user.js into the editor and save. (If running locally instead of against http://cprecall.duckdns.org, update BACKEND_URL and FRONTEND_URL at the top of the script.)
  4. Log into the CP Recall web dashboard (http://cprecall.duckdns.org), click the Extension Key button in the top header (TopHeader.jsx) to copy your JWT, open any LeetCode problem, paste the key into the widget's Extension Key input, and click Save.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
1. SPA & session tracking: Records sessionStart when a problem page opens and uses a MutationObserver on document.body to detect LeetCode SPA navigation between problems and reset state.
  2. Baseline management: Fetches the existing submission list on page load and stores lastSeenTopId so pre-session submissions are excluded.
  3. Submission polling: Polls LeetCode's GraphQL API every 4 seconds (setInterval(..., 4000)) for new submissions, collecting every non-pending attempt (Wrong Answer, Time Limit Exceeded, Accepted, etc.) into submissionHistory[].
  4. Code extraction: When the latest new submission reaches Accepted, stops polling and fetches the full source code, language, runtime, and memory via submissionDetails.
  5. LLM analysis: Calls POST /api/analyze via GM_xmlhttpRequest and renders the Efficiency Score, complexity comparison, and richAnalysis cards inside the floating widget.
  6. Manual hint count & ingestion: Provides a numeric Hints Used input field (default 0) — hint usage is not automatically detected or tracked by the extension. When the user clicks Submit to CPRecal, the extension sends the session, submission history, accepted code, hintsUsed, and analysisResult to POST /api/ingestion/submission.

docs.title: Authentication (JWT Flow)
docs.text:
The extension has no independent login form. It uses a manual token-transfer flow:

  1. The user authenticates on the CP Recall dashboard, which stores their JWT in localStorage (cprecall_token) and an HTTP-only cookie.
  2. Clicking Extension Key in the dashboard header copies that JWT to the clipboard.
  3. Pasting and saving the key in the Tampermonkey widget stores it in Tampermonkey's persistent storage via GM_setValue("cprecall_sync_token", val).
  4. getAuthHeaders() reads GM_getValue("cprecall_sync_token", null) and attaches Authorization: Bearer <token> to POST /api/analyze and POST /api/ingestion/submission.
  5. Cross-origin requests use GM_xmlhttpRequest (declared with @grant and @connect *) to bypass LeetCode's Content Security Policy and cookie restrictions, with a fetch() fallback if GM_xmlhttpRequest is unavailable.

docs.title: LeetCode GraphQL Integration
docs.text:
Three separate GraphQL operations are executed against https://leetcode.com/graphql/:

Operation Data Retrieved questionData questionId, questionFrontendId, title, titleSlug, difficulty, topicTags (does not fetch problem description) submissionList Recent submission id, status, statusDisplay, lang, runtime, memory, timestamp, isPending submissionDetails runtime, memory, code, statusCode, lang { name verboseName }

docs.title: Extension State
docs.text: Variable Purpose currentTitleSlug Slug of the active LeetCode problem sessionStartTime Timestamp when the problem session began lastSeenTopId Most recent submission ID at session start (baseline) submissionHistory Array of all new non-pending submissions detected in this session acceptedDetected Flag preventing duplicate processing once Accepted is reached pollInterval Reference to the 4-second polling interval

docs.title: Floating Widget UI
docs.text:
The extension injects a draggable dark-themed floating overlay (#cr-widget) that can be minimized to a compact bubble (position persisted via GM_setValue("CPRecal_widget_pos")). It transitions through three states:

  • Waiting / Tracking: Displays session status pulse, Extension Key link/input badge (● Connected / ○ Not Linked), problem title, difficulty, and tags.
  • Solved: Displays time taken, submissions until success, runtime, memory, live Gemini analysis results, the manual Hints Used numeric input, and Submit to CPRecal.
  • Submitted: Displays the backend-computed Mastery Score and Next Review date, with a direct link to the dashboard.

docs.title: Stack
docs.text: React 18 + Vite single-page application, served separately from the backend API.

docs.title: Application Shell and Routing
docs.text:
App.jsx defines two routing zones:

  • Public routes (/login, /register): wrapped in PublicRoute — redirect to / if the user is already authenticated
  • Protected routes (/, /patterns, /problems, /problems/:id): wrapped in ProtectedRoute + AppShell — redirect to /login if not authenticated

The AppShell renders the sidebar, top header, mobile drawer, and an <Outlet> for the active page.

docs.title: Home (/)
docs.text: The command centre view: - Stats bar: problems solved, patterns covered, today's recall count, average mastery - Today's Revision: list of recall-due problems (Problem B, not the original triggers), with a "Mark Done" button that fires POST /api/reviews with status: completed - Targeted Practice Recommendations: unsolved problems in the user's weakest patterns - Weak/Strong Patterns: the bottom-3 and top-3 pattern masteries - Spaced Recall Architecture card: explains the FSRS logic to the user

docs.title: Pattern Dashboard (/patterns)
docs.text: Mastery across all 25 tracked DSA patterns: - Filterable by status (Recall Due, Scheduled, Attempted, Unsolved) and by mastery tier (Mastered ≥80%, Strong ≥60%, Moderate ≥40%, Needs Focus <40%) - Sortable by mastery (asc/desc), problems solved, or name - Each pattern card shows: mastery %, problems solved, next recall date, strength tier badge - Sidebar sections for top-3 strongest and top-3 weakest patterns

docs.title: Problem Library (/problems)
docs.text: Full problem catalog with user-specific state overlaid: - Filters: difficulty, status (Solved, Unsolved, Recall Due, Scheduled), pattern, text search - Pagination: 20 problems per page; filter params synced to URL query string - Each card shows: title, difficulty badge, pattern tags, mastery %, recall status, LeetCode link, Problem Details link

docs.title: Problem Details (/problems/:id)
docs.text: Deep view of a single problem: - Problem header: LeetCode ID, title, difficulty, pattern tags - Mastery ring (circular progress indicator showing overall mastery %) - Mastery breakdown: 5 component scores with progress bars - Solving data: time taken, submission count, language, solve date - FSRS state: current interval, next review date, ease factor - LLM Analysis panel: actual vs optimal complexity + rich pedagogical breakdown (all 7 richAnalysis fields from Gemini) - Accepted solution code with copy button - Unsolved state: prompt to solve on LeetCode with the extension active

docs.title: Auth Pages (/login, /register)
docs.text: Standard form-based authentication. Register requires name, email, password, confirm password — client-side password mismatch validation runs before any API call.

docs.title: State Management
docs.text: No global state library. State is managed via: - AuthContext: user object, token, login/logout/register functions, loading state - ThemeContext: light/dark theme preference persisted to localStorage - Local useState/useEffect per page component

docs.title: What is This Scheduler?
docs.text:
FSRS (Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler) is an open-source spaced repetition family that models memory using separate Difficulty, Stability, and Retrievability (DSR) parameters.

CP Recall does not implement the full FSRS-4.5/5 DSR mathematical model. Instead, scheduler.js and ratingMapper.js implement a simplified, FSRS-inspired custom scheduler adapted for DSA pattern learning — mapping mastery scores to 1–4 ratings, assigning fixed initial intervals (1, 3, 7, or 14 days), and scaling subsequent intervals with a per-problem easeFactor clamped to [1.3, 2.5].

docs.title: Ease Factor
docs.text: A per-problem multiplier (default: 2.5, minimum: 1.3) that scales the review interval. Higher ease factor means longer intervals, implying the concept is easy for this user.

docs.title: Review Interval
docs.text: The number of days before the next review is due. Starts at the initial interval determined by the mastery rating and grows multiplicatively on each successful review.

docs.title: Next Review Date
docs.text: Stored as nextReviewDate = today + intervalDays. The dashboard queries all FSRSState records where nextReviewDate ≤ today to surface due reviews.

docs.title: On First Solve
docs.text:
mastery → FSRS rating (1–4) → initialInterval

FSRSState created:
  rating          = derived from mastery
  intervalDays    = initialInterval
  easeFactor      = 2.5
  nextReviewDate  = today + intervalDays

docs.title: On Re-Solve (the user solves the same problem again)
docs.text:
if rating ≥ 3 (Good/Excellent):
    newInterval = ceil(existingInterval × easeFactor)
    easeFactor  = min(2.5, easeFactor + 0.1)

elif rating == 2 (Moderate):
    newInterval = ceil(existingInterval × 1.2)
    (easeFactor unchanged)

else (rating == 1, Learn):
    newInterval = initialInterval for this rating
    easeFactor  = max(1.3, easeFactor − 0.2)

docs.title: On Review Submission (POST /api/reviews)
docs.text:
"completed": newInterval = ceil(interval × easeFactor), easeFactor += 0.1
"failed":    newInterval = initialInterval, easeFactor −= 0.2
"skipped":   newInterval = 1 day

docs.title: Why a Custom Adaptive Scheduler Instead of Fixed-Interval SM-2?
docs.text: Basic fixed-multiplier schedules do not adapt well without manual user difficulty ratings. CP Recall's custom scheduler derives the 1–4 rating automatically from the 5-component mastery score and adjusts the per-problem easeFactor (1.3 to 2.5) over time, separating strong patterns (long intervals) from weak ones (short intervals) without requiring manual flashcard grading.

docs.title: Interval Growth Example
docs.text:
For a user who consistently scores Excellent (rating 4):

Review Interval easeFactor Initial 14 days 2.5 After review 1 35 days 2.5 After review 2 87 days 2.5

For a user who struggles (rating 1 → 2):

Review Interval easeFactor Initial 1 day 2.5 Re-rated to 2 3 days 2.3 Re-rated to 1 1 day 1.3

docs.title: Separation of Trigger and Target
docs.text:
A critical architectural decision: the FSRSState is associated with the solved problem (Problem A) — not the problem being recalled. When A is due, the system uses A's patterns to find a different Problem B. This ensures the user is never asked to repeat Problem A from memory.

See the Recall Engine page for details.

docs.title: Manual Extension Installation & JWT Copy-Paste
docs.text: Users must manually install Tampermonkey, add code/extension/cp-recal.user.js, copy their JWT via the dashboard's Extension Key button, and paste it into the extension widget. There is no automated one-click browser store install or OAuth token exchange.

docs.title: Manual Hint Tracking
docs.text: The extension does not automatically detect whether or how many LeetCode hints the user viewed. Users manually enter Hints Used (default 0) in the widget before submitting, so the accuracy of the 15% Hints Used mastery component relies on user self-reporting.

docs.title: Problem Description Availability on First Solve
docs.text: The extension's questionData GraphQL query does not fetch problem descriptions, and processSubmission.js does not populate Problem.description. Although analyzeController.js lazy-loads the description from LeetCode's questionContent GraphQL endpoint when a Problem record already exists in the database without one, that lazy-load is skipped if the problem is not yet in the database when /api/analyze runs (for example, the first time any user solves a newly added problem).

docs.title: Plain HTTP Deployment Endpoint
docs.text: The confirmed AWS EC2 deployment URL (http://cprecall.duckdns.org) serves traffic over plain HTTP rather than HTTPS, so requests (including JWTs and code payloads) are not TLS-encrypted in transit at that endpoint.

docs.title: Unspecified AWS Region in Repository Config
docs.text: While the live AWS EC2 deployment URL (http://cprecall.duckdns.org) is confirmed, the production AWS region is not recorded in repository configuration (.env.example uses ap-southeast-2 only as an example placeholder).

docs.title: Simplified FSRS-Inspired Scheduler
docs.text: The implemented scheduler (scheduler.js) uses a simplified interval-and-ease-factor model rather than the full FSRS-4.5/5 DSR algorithm (which models separate Difficulty, Stability, and Retrievability parameters). It does not reproduce full FSRS interval curves.

docs.title: Pattern Assignment
docs.text: Algorithmic patterns are assigned to problems by the extension (sent as part of the ingestion payload). The accuracy of pattern assignment depends on the quality of the data provided at solve time. There is no server-side pattern validation or correction.

docs.title: Optimal Complexity Ground Truth & Fallback
docs.text: The "optimal" time and space complexity used for the Solution Efficiency and Time Complexity scores is provided by Gemini 2.0 Flash, not by a curated database of verified optimal solutions. Gemini's assessment may occasionally be incorrect for atypical problems, and if any complexity field is missing from Gemini's JSON output, codeAnalysis.js falls back to "O(N)", which can distort the resulting mastery score.

docs.title: No Offline Mode
docs.text: The dashboard and extension require active internet connectivity. There is no offline caching of review schedules or problem data beyond the client-side 15-second API cache.

docs.title: Progress Reset (DynamoDB Only)
docs.text: The atomic, concurrency-safe progress reset with verification (progressResetService.js) is fully implemented for DynamoDB only. The MongoDB code path does not have the same multi-step deletion with locking.

docs.title: Single Accepted Solution Per Problem
docs.text: AcceptedSolution is upserted on re-solve — a later solve overwrites the earlier one. Only the most recent accepted code and analysis are stored per (user, problem) pair.

docs.title: Future Scope
docs.text:
• Full FSRS-5 implementation: Incorporate the complete FSRS-5 algorithm with separate stability/difficulty parameters for more accurate scheduling
  • Automated extension installation: One-click extension install with OAuth-based token exchange instead of manual JWT configuration
  • Server-side pattern curation: A verified pattern-to-problem mapping maintained server-side, reducing dependence on extension-provided pattern data
  • Multi-platform support: Extend beyond LeetCode to Codeforces, HackerRank, etc.
  • Social/team features: Compare mastery across team members, shared problem lists
  • Mobile application: React Native app for review notifications
  • Offline review mode: Cache due problems locally for offline sessions
  • End-to-end testing: Playwright test suite covering full solving → review cycles

docs.title: Mastery Scoring Algorithm
docs.text: When a user solves a problem on LeetCode, CP Recall computes a mastery score from 0 to 100 that reflects the quality of the solution across five dimensions.

docs.title: 1. Solution Efficiency (SE) — weight 25%
docs.text:
Compares the user's actual time and space complexity against the optimal complexity determined by Gemini's analysis.

Scenario Score TC matches optimal AND SC matches optimal 100 TC matches, SC does not 90 TC does not match, SC does 70 Neither matches 60

Formula: score = 100 − TC_penalty − SC_penalty (TC_penalty = 30, SC_penalty = 10)

docs.title: 2. Time Complexity (TC) — weight 25%
docs.text: Scenario Score User's TC == optimal TC 100 User's TC is worse than optimal 75

docs.title: Why Solution Efficiency and Time Complexity Are Separate Components
docs.text:
Although both Solution Efficiency (25%) and Time Complexity (25%) inspect the user's time complexity, they serve distinct scoring roles in scoring.js:

  • Solution Efficiency evaluates joint resource optimality across both time and space (-30 if TC is non-optimal, -10 if SC is non-optimal).
  • Time Complexity isolates asymptotic time optimality alone (100 if exact match, 75 otherwise).

Separating them is a design choice in CPRecall's scoring model that gives asymptotic time complexity higher effective weight in the final score: a non-optimal time complexity loses points in both components, whereas a non-optimal space complexity (e.g., O(N) auxiliary space with optimal O(N) time) only loses 10 points inside Solution Efficiency. Note that these component weights (25% / 25% / 20% / 15% / 15%) and penalty heuristics are heuristic design choices rather than empirically validated parameters.

docs.title: 3. Submissions Until Success (SUS) — weight 20%
docs.text:
SUS = max(0, 100 − (submissionCount − 1) × 20)

Attempts Score 1 (first try) 100 2 80 3 60 4 40 5 20 ≥ 6 0

docs.title: 4. Time Taken (TT) — weight 15%
docs.text:
Difficulty Baseline Easy 5 minutes Medium 15 minutes Hard 30 minutes

If minutes ≤ baseline: score = 100. Otherwise: score = min(100, max(0, 100 / (minutes / baseline))).

docs.title: 5. Hints Used (HU) — weight 15%
docs.text:
HU = max(0, 100 − hintsUsed × 15)

Note on hint tracking: Hint usage is not automatically detected or tracked by the extension. Instead, the user manually enters the number of hints used in the Tampermonkey widget's numeric Hints Used field (default 0) before clicking Submit to CPRecal. That manually entered integer is passed to scoring.js for this calculation.

docs.title: Final Mastery Formula
docs.text:
mastery = round(
    SE  × 0.25 +
    TC  × 0.25 +
    SUS × 0.20 +
    TT  × 0.15 +
    HU  × 0.15
)

Result is an integer from 0 to 100.

docs.title: Mastery → FSRS Rating Mapping
docs.text: Mastery FSRS Rating Label Initial Review Interval 0–39 1 Learn 1 day 40–59 2 Moderate 3 days 60–79 3 Good 7 days 80–100 4 Excellent 14 days

docs.title: Pattern Mastery Aggregation
docs.text:
After ProblemMastery is saved, PatternMastery is recomputed for every pattern on the solved problem:

  1. Find all problems in the catalog with this pattern
  2. Find all ProblemMastery records for this user on those problems
  3. avgMastery = sum(mastery) / count(solved)
  4. Average each component score across all solved problems in this pattern
  5. Upsert the PatternMastery record

Pattern mastery is a running aggregate that updates with every new solve.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
Competitive programmers and students preparing for technical interviews face a consistent challenge: they solve large numbers of problems but fail to retain the underlying algorithmic patterns weeks or months later.

This manifests in three ways:

  • A student solves a Sliding Window problem today but cannot recognise a new Sliding Window problem during an interview three weeks later
  • A student has solved 300 LeetCode problems but still fails medium-difficulty problems because pattern recognition has not been internalised
  • A student correctly solves a problem but does not know why a particular approach worked, making it impossible to apply the technique to a variant

docs.title: Motivation and Design Gaps Addressed
docs.text: CP Recall was designed to address specific workflow gaps observed when practicing algorithmic problems across separate tools:

docs.title: Practice Platforms (e.g. LeetCode)
docs.text: Standard coding platforms focus primarily on acceptance status and problem counts. CP Recall's design objective is to add a layer that tracks how efficiently a problem was solved, aggregates performance by algorithmic pattern, and prompts timed reviews of weak patterns.

docs.title: General-Purpose Spaced Repetition (e.g. Anki)
docs.text: Flashcard-based spaced repetition tools are typically built around manually authored cards and self-graded recall. CP Recall is designed to integrate directly into the coding workflow, compute ratings from objective session metrics (complexity, attempts, time, and hints), and recommend a fresh problem rather than repeating the same prompt.

docs.title: Manual Notes and Spreadsheets
docs.text: Tracking solved problems in spreadsheets requires manual upkeep and does not automate review scheduling or pattern-level weakness detection. CP Recall automates session capture and computes pattern aggregates directly from submitted solutions.

docs.title: Proposed Solution
docs.text:
CP Recall creates a pattern-level memory layer over a user's LeetCode activity.

Instead of tracking raw problem counts, it:

  1. Associates each solved problem with its algorithmic pattern(s)
  2. Measures how well the solution demonstrates mastery of that pattern
  3. Uses a simplified FSRS-inspired spaced-repetition scheduler to schedule reviews at adaptive intervals
  4. When a review is due, presents a different, unsolved problem from the same pattern family — testing pattern transfer on a problem the user has not yet solved, rather than repeating the original problem

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Automatically capture problem-solving sessions, code, and submission attempts from LeetCode (with only optional manual hint count input)
  • Compute a nuanced mastery score from multiple performance dimensions
  • Schedule pattern-level reviews using FSRS spaced repetition
  • Surface the right problem at the right time to maximise long-term retention
  • Provide a dashboard that makes the user's pattern-level weaknesses immediately visible
  • Support multiple users with fully isolated progress tracking

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The core pedagogical insight of CP Recall is that reviewing a concept is best done by solving a different, unsolved problem that exercises the same pattern — not by re-solving the original problem from memory. (Note: the engine filters out problems the user has already solved in ProblemMastery, the trigger Problem A, and duplicates within the same batch; it does not track or exclude problems the user may have merely viewed or attempted without solving.)

The Recall Engine (recallSelector.js) dynamically resolves a "target" Problem B for every "trigger" Problem A that is due for FSRS review.

docs.title: Algorithm
docs.text:
Input:  fsrsTriggers[]  — FSRSState records where nextReviewDate ≤ today
        userId          — authenticated user

Output: resolvedTargets[] — {problem: B, originalDueProblemId: A, relevantPattern, ...}

Step 1 — Pre-load solved problem IDs Query all ProblemMastery records for the user → extract problemId set.

Step 2 — Pre-load pattern masteries Query all PatternMastery records → build Map<pattern, mastery>. This avoids N+1 database round-trips when processing many triggers.

Step 3 — For each trigger Problem A:

a. Extract A's patterns array

b. Map each pattern to its mastery score from the pre-loaded map (O(1) lookup)

c. Sort patterns ascending by mastery → select the weakest pattern

d. Determine target difficulty: - Weakest pattern mastery < 50% → Easy - 50% ≤ mastery < 80% → Medium - mastery ≥ 80% → Hard

e. Query problem catalog: patterns contains weakest_pattern AND difficulty = target excluding (solved IDs ∪ {A} ∪ already-selected-in-this-batch)

f. If no difficulty match found: fall back to any difficulty, same pattern, same exclusions

g. If still no candidates: return empty — never fall back to Problem A

h. Shuffle candidates, pick one at random

i. Add selected problem to selectedRecallProblemIds set (batch deduplication — prevents the same Problem B from being selected for multiple triggers in one request)

j. Build result: { problem: B, originalDueProblemId: A, relevantPattern, relevantMastery, nextReviewDate }

Step 4 — Return resolvedTargets[]

docs.title: Exhaustion Handling
docs.text: If the user has solved every problem in a given pattern (catalog exhaustion), the engine returns no target for that trigger. A LibraryCompletionModal is shown if the user has solved every problem in the entire catalog (totalSolved === totalProblems), prompting them to reset progress and start a new learning cycle.

docs.title: Performance Decisions
docs.text: Decision Reason Pre-load pattern mastery map O(1) per lookup vs O(N) per trigger Pre-load solved IDs as Set O(1) exclusion checks DynamoDB in-memory catalog Catalog queries operate from RAM (no remote I/O per lookup) Batch deduplication set Prevents same Problem B being assigned to multiple triggers

docs.title: Why Pattern-Level, Not Problem-Level?
docs.text: If the FSRS trigger were attached to individual problems and the user were shown the same problem on review, they would be testing recall of the solution rather than recognition of the pattern. By selecting a structurally similar but visually different problem, the system tests genuine conceptual transfer.

docs.title: Application Workflow
docs.text: This page describes the complete end-to-end flow from a user solving a problem on LeetCode through to the system scheduling the next review.

docs.title: Full Solving Session Flow
docs.text:
User opens a LeetCode problem
         │
         ▼
Extension detects the problem page
• Records sessionStart timestamp
• Fetches problem metadata via GraphQL (without description)
• Fetches existing submissions via GraphQL
• Stores lastSeenTopId as a baseline to exclude pre-session submissions
         │
         ▼
User submits a solution
         │
         ▼
Extension polls LeetCode GraphQL every 4 seconds for new submissions
• Compares each submission's ID against lastSeenTopId
• Collects all new submissions (WA, TLE, MLE, Accepted) into submissionHistory[]
• Resets tracking state if the user navigates to a different problem
         │
         ▼
Submission is Accepted
         │
         ├── Extension fetches accepted code via GraphQL (submissionDetails)
         │
         ├── POST /api/analyze ──► Gemini 2.0 Flash
         │
         │   body: { code, problemTitle, difficulty, language, titleSlug }
         │   (backend lazy-loads description from LeetCode if problem exists in DB)
         │
         │   returns:
         │     actualTimeComplexity, actualSpaceComplexity
         │     optimalTimeComplexity, optimalSpaceComplexity
         │     explanation, richAnalysis (7 fields)
         │
         ├── User optionally enters Hints Used (manual numeric input, default 0)
         │   and clicks "Submit to CPRecal"
         │
         ▼
POST /api/ingestion/submission  (Bearer token via GM_xmlhttpRequest)
{
  problemId, title, titleSlug, difficulty, patterns,
  sessionStart, sessionEnd, submissionHistory[],
  acceptedSubmissionId, acceptedCode, language, hintsUsed, analysisResult
}
         │
         ▼
processSubmission() — 9-step pipeline
  Step 1: Find or create Problem record (by leetcodeId)
  Step 2: Create SolvingSession (totalTimeSeconds computed)
  Step 3: Batch-create Submission records for each attempt
  Step 4: Upsert AcceptedSolution (code + analysis)
  Step 5: Calculate ProblemMastery (5-component weighted score)
  Step 6: Update PatternMastery for each pattern on this problem
  Step 7: Create/update FSRSState (nextReviewDate, intervalDays, easeFactor)
  Step 8: Create ReviewHistory entry
  Step 9: Return structured result

docs.title: Review Surfacing Flow
docs.text:
User opens the CP Recall dashboard (/)
         │
         ▼
GET /api/dashboard → dashboardService.getDashboardData(userId)

  Parallel queries:
  • User stats (solved count, average mastery, attempt count)
  • All pattern masteries → weak/strong pattern rankings
  • FSRSState: all triggers where nextReviewDate ≤ today
  • Problem catalog batch fetch
         │
         ▼
selectRecallTargets(dueProblems, userId)

  For each due trigger Problem A:
    • Look up A's patterns
    • Find the weakest pattern (lowest mastery in patternMasteryMap)
    • Determine target difficulty from pattern mastery
    • Query catalog for unsolved Problem B in that pattern
    • Return B annotated with originalDueProblemId: A
         │
         ▼
todaysRevision array displayed on Home dashboard
User sees: "Problem B — Sliding Window — Recall Due"
         │
User clicks "Mark Done"
         │
POST /api/reviews { problemId: A, status: "completed", satisfiedByProblemId: B }
  → interval updated, nextReviewDate pushed forward

docs.title: Targeted Practice Flow (Recommendations)
docs.text:
GET /api/recommendations
  • Fetches user's pattern masteries
  • Identifies weakest patterns
  • Queries problem catalog for unsolved problems in those patterns
  • Returns unsolved problems (excluding problems in the user's `ProblemMastery` records), ordered by weak pattern priority
